lessons.title: Goodness of fit with a specified discrete model
lessons.summary: Compare complete frequency patterns, using model probabilities rather than observed proportions.
lessons.objective: Form hypotheses, calculate Pearson’s statistic and test a fully specified categorical or discrete model.
lessons.before: Review binomial and Poisson probabilities, expected frequencies and significance tests.
lessons.ideas:
State a model, not an observed equality

H₀ states that the population follows the specified probability model. H₁ states that it does not. Sampling variation normally makes observed and expected frequencies different even under H₀; the question is whether the discrepancy is too large to attribute to that model.

From probability to frequency

\[\begin{gathered}E_i=Np_i\\X^2=\sum_i\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}.\end{gathered}\]

The categories must be disjoint and cover every possible outcome. Each independent observation belongs to exactly one category. The counts, not percentages or density heights, enter the statistic. Expected counts sum to N, but need not be integers.

For a binomial model, \(p_j=\binom mjp^j(1-p)^{m-j}\). For a Poisson model, \(p_j=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^j/j!\). An open final class such as X≥k uses the entire tail \(1-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}p_j\), including unobserved possibilities.

Pool first, then calculate

Use the course convention that each final expected count is at least 5. If necessary combine adjacent count classes, combining both their observed and expected frequencies. Do not discard a sparse tail or select a grouping to obtain a preferred conclusion. A zero observed count alone does not require pooling.

Degrees of freedom and the upper tail

For k final classes and no parameter estimated from the test sample, ν=k−1. The total-frequency constraint removes one freely varying count. Under the null and the expected-count conditions, X² is approximately χ² with ν degrees of freedom. Large discrepancies give large non-negative values; rejection is in the upper tail.

Compare with the upper α critical value, or reject when the upper-tail p-value is at most α. Otherwise there is insufficient evidence against the model; this is not proof it is true. Keep full precision until the final reported statistic.
lessons.method:
1. Define the population model and hypotheses.
  2. List all categories and obtain their probabilities, including tails.
  3. Multiply by N and pool using expected counts.
  4. Calculate each Pearson contribution for the final classes and add.
  5. Use k−1 degrees of freedom, the upper tail and a contextual conclusion.
mistakes: Divide the squared difference by E, not O.
Check expected counts, not observed counts, when deciding to pool.
An unobserved model tail can have positive probability.
Failure to reject does not establish that the model is correct.

examples.title: 1 · A categorical specification
examples.question: A booking system should send requests to channels A, B and C with probabilities \(1/2,1/3,1/6\). For 120 independent requests the observed frequencies are 54, 44 and 22. Test the specification at 5%, using the supplied critical value 5.991.
examples.solution:
\[E=(60,40,20).\]\[X^2=\frac{36}{60}+\frac{16}{40}+\frac4{20}=\frac65.\]

All expected counts exceed 5. No parameter was estimated, so ν=3−1=2. Since 1.2<5.991, do not reject. There is insufficient evidence at 5% that the channel probabilities differ from the specification.

examples.title: 2 · A complete fixed binomial model
examples.question: Three independent opportunities occur in each run, each with specified success probability 1/2. For 80 independent runs, the frequencies of 0,1,2,3 successes are 8,28,31,13. Find the expected frequencies, statistic and degrees of freedom.
examples.solution:
Under H₀ the count follows B(3,1/2), so the probabilities are (1,3,3,1)/8.

\[E=(10,30,30,10).\]\[X^2=\frac4{10}+\frac4{30}+\frac1{30}+\frac9{10}=\frac{22}{15}.\]

All four expectations are at least 5, and the probability was fixed independently. Thus ν=4−1=3. A test decision would also require a significance level.

examples.title: 3 · Pool the sparse expected tail
examples.question: Six ordered count classes have observed frequencies (32,32,21,10,3,2) and specified expected frequencies (35,30,20,9,4,2). Combine the last two classes before calculating the statistic.
examples.solution:
The last expectations 4 and 2 are below 5; together they give 6. Pool the observed frequencies in exactly the same way.

\[\begin{gathered}O=(32,32,21,10,5)\\E=(35,30,20,9,6).\end{gathered}\]\[X^2=\frac9{35}+\frac4{30}+\frac1{20}+\frac19+\frac16=\frac{181}{252}.\]

There are now five classes, so ν=4. Do not add the two original Pearson contributions: pooling changes the contribution.

examples.title: 4 · The p-value is an upper-tail area
examples.question: A valid Pearson test has statistic 6 and 2 degrees of freedom. Its upper-tail probability is \(e^{-3}\), approximately 0.0498. State the decisions at 5% and 1%.
examples.solution: Reject at 5%, since \(e^{-3}<0.05\); do not reject at 1%, since \(e^{-3}>0.01\). For 2 degrees of freedom, the survival probability at x is \(e^{-x/2}\). This is a probability of a statistic at least as large under H₀, not a probability that H₀ is true.

lessons.title: Discrete models with a fitted parameter
lessons.summary: Estimate from the original data and account for the information used in fitting.
lessons.objective: Fit Poisson or binomial models, pool correctly and adjust the degrees of freedom.
lessons.before: Complete specified-model goodness of fit. Review frequency-weighted means and sample variance.
lessons.ideas:
Keep estimation separate from the test

\[\begin{gathered}\widehat\lambda=\bar x=\frac{\sum xf}{N}\\\widehat p=\frac{\bar x}{m}\\\text{for B}(m,p).\end{gathered}\]

Estimate from the original observations or full original frequency table before pooling. The sample size N counts independent runs, panels or packages; m counts trials within each one. A grouped tail with non-zero frequency does not determine an exact mean unless its individual values or a total are supplied.

Use the fitted model at full precision

Calculate all expected counts from the unrounded fitted parameter, including the complete tail. Then choose defensible pooled classes using their expected counts. Matching a sample mean and variance can suggest a model to investigate, but it does not test its whole shape or establish independent trials.

Fitting uses degrees of freedom

\[\nu=k-1-s,\]

Here k counts final pooled classes, and s is the number of distributional parameters estimated from the same sample for the model. One fitted Poisson mean or one fitted binomial success probability costs one degree of freedom. A value specified independently does not, even if it happens to equal the estimate you would have obtained. The fixed number of binomial trials is not a fitted parameter.

The subtraction reflects additional constraints imposed by fitting, beyond the total count. Check ν is positive and the final expected counts satisfy the approximation conditions. The hypotheses concern membership of the distributional family; they are not a claim that the unknown parameter equals its numerical sample estimate.

Explain a poor fit in context

A binomial model requires a fixed number of trials, a common success probability and independent trial outcomes within a run. Shared damage or variable conditions can break these assumptions even when different sampled objects are independent. A Poisson model also needs suitable count-rate assumptions for equal exposure periods.
lessons.method:
1. Identify which parameters come from this sample.
  2. Fit them using the full original observations.
  3. Calculate unrounded model expectations and pool suitably.
  4. Find X² and ν=k−1−s.
  5. Use the upper-tail test and assess the model in the original context.
mistakes: Estimate before pooling; do not replace tail values by an arbitrary midpoint.
Do not round a fitted probability before calculating expected counts.
Count only parameters fitted from the test sample.
A similar mean and variance do not establish a Poisson distribution.

examples.title: 1 · Estimate from a complete count table
examples.question: Forty independent operating sessions produce counts 0,1,2,3,4 with frequencies 9,16,10,4,1. There are no larger observed counts. Estimate a Poisson mean and calculate the unbiased sample variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum xf=52\\\sum x^2f=108\\\widehat\lambda=\frac{13}{10}.\end{gathered}\]\[s^2=\frac{108-52^2/40}{39}=\frac{202}{195}.\]

The observed variance is fairly near the mean, but a complete goodness-of-fit test must compare all expected class frequencies and retain the Poisson tail beyond 4.

examples.title: 2 · Distinguish runs from trials
examples.question: Each of 50 independent runs has four trials. The observed numbers of successes 0,1,2,3,4 have frequencies 5,15,18,10,2. Estimate the common binomial success probability.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum xf=89\\\bar x=\frac{89}{50}\\\widehat p=\frac{89}{50\cdot4}=\frac{89}{200}.\end{gathered}\]

There are 50 observed counts, containing 200 underlying trial outcomes. The expected frequency for zero successes would be \(50(111/200)^4\), using the fitted value without early rounding.

examples.title: 3 · A fitted value can look like a specification
examples.question: For 100 independent runs with three trials each, the frequencies of 0,1,2,3 successes are (8,42,42,8). Fit a binomial model and test it at 5%, using the supplied critical value 5.991.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=\frac{150}{100}=\frac32\\\widehat p=\frac12.\end{gathered}\]\[E=(12.5,37.5,37.5,12.5).\]\[X^2=2\left(\frac{4.5^2}{12.5}+\frac{4.5^2}{37.5}\right)=\frac{108}{25}.\]

No pooling is needed. The value 1/2 was estimated here, not specified in advance: ν=4−1−1=2. Since 4.32<5.991, do not reject this binomial family at 5%.

examples.title: 4 · Count final classes, then fitted parameters
examples.question: A goodness-of-fit analysis has eight original classes. Pooling leaves six. Find ν when one parameter was fitted from the sample, and when the same model parameter was instead specified independently.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\nu_{\mathrm{fitted}}=6-1-1=4\\\nu_{\mathrm{specified}}=6-1=5.\end{gathered}\]

Use six final classes, not eight original classes. The source of the parameter, not merely its numerical value, determines the extra subtraction.

lessons.title: Goodness of fit for continuous distributions
lessons.summary: Calculate class probabilities from areas or a CDF and retain the entire model support.
lessons.objective: Test supplied or fitted continuous models with correct boundaries, tails and degrees of freedom.
lessons.ideas:
Expected counts use probability areas

\[\begin{gathered}p_i=\int_{a_i}^{b_i}f(x)\,dx=F(b_i)-F(a_i)\\E_i=Np_i.\end{gathered}\]

A density at the midpoint is a height, not the probability of the class. Unequal widths must be reflected by the integrals. Classes cover the model support without gaps or overlap; for a continuous distribution, changing inclusion of a single endpoint does not change its probability.

Unobserved tails still count

A normal model has support across the real line. If no observation lies beyond the finite recorded range, those tail observations have frequency zero, but the model still allocates positive probability there. Extend the extreme classes to infinity or include explicit outside classes, then pool if necessary. Do not renormalise only over the observed range unless a genuinely truncated model was specified.

For a normal model, standardise a boundary by \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\), then subtract cumulative probabilities. Include lower and upper tails. Check all expected counts together sum to N before computing Pearson’s statistic.

How many parameters were fitted?

Use ν=k−1−s for k final classes. For a normal model, s=0 when both mean and variance were specified independently, s=1 when just one was estimated from this sample, and s=2 when both were. Standard deviation and variance represent the same one scale parameter, not two separate ones. A grouped mean calculated only as a descriptive comparison does not make a previously fixed model parameter fitted.

When supplied fitted values are to be used, retain them; do not silently replace them with a midpoint estimate. Pearson’s test here is an upper-tail approximation, with all final expectations at least 5. A failure to reject does not demonstrate normality or identify a unique density.
lessons.method:
1. Write the complete support and every class boundary.
  2. Find probabilities by integrating the density or subtracting CDF values.
  3. Check total probability 1 and multiply by N.
  4. Pool suitably, calculate X² and subtract the parameters fitted from this sample.
  5. Use the upper tail and interpret the full distributional model.
mistakes: Do not substitute a density height for a probability.
Do not truncate a normal tail just because it contains no observed reading.
Use actual boundaries, including any stated measurement rounding.
A normal mean and standard deviation fitted together cost two degrees of freedom.

examples.title: 1 · Integrate over the class
examples.question: A specified density is \(f(x)=x/2\) on [0,2], zero elsewhere. Eighty independent readings give 18 in [0,1) and 62 in [1,2]. Find the expected counts and test statistic.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p_1=\int_0^1\frac x2\,dx=\frac14\\p_2=\frac34.\end{gathered}\]\[\begin{gathered}E=(20,60)\\X^2=\frac4{20}+\frac4{60}=\frac4{15}\\\nu=1.\end{gathered}\]

The total density area is 1. There are two final classes and no fitted parameters. The density height at x=1 is not the first-class probability.

examples.title: 2 · Unequal widths need unequal expectations
examples.question: A model is uniform on [0,10]. In 100 independent readings, the counts in [0,1), [1,4) and [4,10] are 8,33,59. Find the model expectations, statistic and degrees of freedom.
examples.solution:
\[E=100\left(\frac1{10},\frac3{10},\frac6{10}\right)=(10,30,60).\]\[\begin{gathered}X^2=\frac4{10}+\frac9{30}+\frac1{60}=\frac{43}{60}\\\nu=2.\end{gathered}\]

Equal density does not imply equal probability for unequal-width intervals.

examples.title: 3 · Keep the whole normal distribution
examples.question: A specification fixes a normal mean of 50 and standard deviation 4. For 100 independent readings, the counts in (−∞,46), [46,50), [50,54) and [54,∞) are 12,35,39,14. Test the model at 5%, using 7.815.
examples.solution:
The standardised boundaries are −1,0,1. CDF differences, including both exterior tails, give

\[E\approx(15.866,34.134,34.134,15.866).\]

Using unrounded probabilities, \(X^2\approx1.877\). Both parameters were specified, so ν=4−1=3. All expectations exceed 5 and the statistic is below 7.815: there is insufficient evidence against the specification.

examples.title: 4 · Separate a descriptive mean from fitting
examples.question: A test has seven final classes. Find ν for a normal model when both parameters were estimated from the test sample. What if both were fixed in advance, but you also calculated the sample mean to describe the data?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\nu_{\mathrm{fitted}}=7-1-2=4\\\nu_{\mathrm{fixed}}=7-1=6.\end{gathered}\]

A descriptive sample mean does not change a fixed specification. Only using the sample to fit the model changes s.

lessons.title: Association and contingency tables
lessons.summary: Use the margins to test independence and interpret association without overstating it.
lessons.objective: Calculate expected tables, pool whole categories when justified and test population independence.
lessons.before: Review Pearson’s statistic, proportions and independent sampling. The table entries must count separate observations, not overlapping classifications.
lessons.ideas:
Two categorical variables

Each independent observation receives one row category and one column category. H₀ states that the variables are independent in the population; H₁ states that they are associated. Samples taken separately by row can equivalently test whether the column distributions are the same across those groups.

Why the expected-frequency formula works

Under independence, multiply the estimated row probability Rᵢ/N by the column probability Cⱼ/N and then by N:

\[E_{ij}=N\frac{R_i}{N}\frac{C_j}{N}=\frac{R_iC_j}{N}.\]

Expected row and column totals match the observed margins. They need not be integers. Calculate a contribution for each interior cell, excluding the totals themselves:

\[X^2=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.\]

Degrees of freedom come from the table dimensions

\[\nu=(r-1)(c-1).\]

Given the margins, an upper-left block of (r−1)(c−1) cells determines the remaining row and column entries. Do not use rc−1, and do not subtract another parameter count on top of this formula.

Sparse cells and interpretation

Check every expected count is at least 5. If meaningful categories must be combined, merge an entire row or column consistently, then recalculate margins, expectations and ν. A pre-specified pooling rule prevents selecting categories to obtain a desired conclusion. Do not pool isolated cells into an irregular table.

A significant result supports association, not a measure of its practical size. Compare within-group proportions when group sizes differ. Observational association alone does not establish causation. Failure to reject does not prove independence.

For a genuinely new independent sample with every count multiplied by k, expectations also multiply by k and X² multiplies by k; ν stays unchanged. Copying the old records does not create independent evidence.
lessons.method:
1. Define both categorical variables and the sampling units.
  2. State independence versus association and calculate all margins.
  3. Calculate every expected cell and apply any justified whole-category pooling.
  4. Add Pearson contributions and use (r−1)(c−1) degrees of freedom.
  5. Conclude in context and distinguish evidence, effect size and causation.
mistakes: Use row total × column total ÷ grand total, not a row percentage alone.
Totals are constraints, not extra observations or test cells.
Merge whole categories, not selected isolated cells.
Compare proportions when groups have different sizes.
Duplicated records do not create a larger independent sample.

examples.title: 1 · Complete a two-by-two test
examples.question:
Two independently sampled groups have the following preference counts. Test independence at 5%, using 3.841.

Observed counts
GroupOption AOption B
R1812
S1218
examples.solution:
Both row totals and both column totals are 30; N=60. Every expected count is 30·30/60=15.

\[\begin{gathered}X^2=4\left(\frac{3^2}{15}\right)=\frac{12}{5}\\\nu=1.\end{gathered}\]

Since 2.4<3.841, do not reject independence. The observed preferences differ, but there is insufficient evidence of a population association at 5%.

examples.title: 2 · The dimensions matter
examples.question:
Independent samples from two sites give these service-choice counts. Find the expected table and statistic.

Observed counts
SiteExpressStandardFlexible

examples.solution:
Each row total is 60, the column totals are (30,30,60), and N=120. Each expected row is (15,15,30).

\[\begin{gathered}X^2=4\left(\frac9{15}\right)=\frac{12}{5}\\\nu=(2-1)(3-1)=2.\end{gathered}\]

The zero contributions in the final column still correspond to valid cells. The same statistic with different degrees of freedom would not have the same p-value.

examples.title: 3 · Merge the entire sparse column
examples.question:
Four ordered categories have these counts from independent observations. A pre-specified rule combines the first two columns when the first expected count is below 5. Apply it and calculate the new statistic.

Observed counts
GroupVery lowLowMediumHigh
A191515
B1191010
examples.solution:
The first expected count in each row is 1. Combine both entries of the first column with their neighbours, giving rows (10,15,15) and (20,10,10). Each expected row is (15,12.5,12.5).

\[X^2=2\left(\frac{25}{15}+\frac{6.25}{12.5}+\frac{6.25}{12.5}\right)=\frac{16}{3}.\]

All final expectations exceed 5 and ν=(2−1)(3−1)=2. The category definitions are the same in both rows.

examples.title: 4 · More independent data, unchanged proportions
examples.question: A two-by-three table has X²=12/5. In a new independent sample every cell count is k times as large, with k a positive integer. Using the supplied 5% critical value 5.991, find the least k leading to rejection.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}X^2_{\mathrm{new}}=k\frac{12}{5}\\\nu=2.\end{gathered}\]

For k=2 the statistic is 4.8, below 5.991. For k=3 it is 7.2, above 5.991, so the least k is 3. This is a hypothetical larger independent sample, not copying existing records.
